subject: english-language
topicDisplay: Unit 3 Studying Spoken And Written Language
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: A speech opens and closes with the very same phrase, "We will not be moved." Framing a text this way is best described as:
questions.explain: Beginning and ending with the same idea creates a cyclical (circular) structure.

questions.q: Which phrase uses ALLITERATION?
questions.explain: Repeated initial "s" sounds in "silent slippery snakes slid" is alliteration.

questions.q: Which sentence is a SIMPLE sentence (one main clause)?
options: When she arrived, the show began, although it was late.
Because it rained, we stayed in.
The dog barked and the cat ran.
questions.explain: "The dog barked." has a single main clause, making it a simple sentence.

questions.q: "The snake slid silently across the soft sand." The repeated soft "s" sound is:
questions.explain: Repetition of "s"/soft hissing sounds is sibilance.

questions.q: A poet uses the same line "and still it rained" at the start of every stanza. This deliberate repetition is best called:
questions.explain: A repeated line used for effect across stanzas is a refrain, a form of repetition.

questions.q: "Her smile was as bright as the sun." This is an example of a:
questions.explain: A comparison using "as" is a simile.

questions.q: A writer follows a long, flowing description with the single line: "Everything stopped." Standing alone as its own paragraph, this short sentence creates:
options: A sudden pause and dramatic emphasis
questions.explain: An isolated short sentence after long ones forces a pause and lands with dramatic impact.

questions.q: A dove is used throughout a text to represent peace. Using an object to stand for an idea is:
questions.explain: An object standing for a larger idea (a dove for peace) is symbolism.

questions.q: Which sentence is a COMPOUND sentence (two main clauses joined by a coordinating conjunction)?
options: The rain fell, and the children cheered.
Although it rained, the children cheered.
questions.explain: Two equal main clauses joined by "and" form a compound sentence.

questions.q: "The thunder grumbled and the rain drummed on the roof." Which TWO techniques are combined here?
questions.explain: "Grumbled" personifies the thunder while "drummed" imitates sound (onomatopoeia).

questions.q: A short, abrupt sentence such as "He ran." placed among long ones is used to:
questions.explain: A short sentence among longer ones creates emphasis and impact.

questions.q: "He gave a warm welcome and a cold farewell." The contrast between "warm" and "cold" placed in the same line is an example of:
questions.explain: Setting opposing words side by side for contrast is juxtaposition (here, antithesis).

questions.q: In a story, a storm rages whenever the hero is angry. The weather reflecting emotion is:
questions.explain: Using weather/nature to mirror a character's mood is pathetic fallacy.

questions.q: "The forest was a cathedral of green." The comparison of the forest to a cathedral mainly creates a sense of:
questions.explain: A cathedral connotes height, quiet and awe, so the metaphor lends the forest grandeur and reverence.

questions.q: What does it mean to say language 'changes over time'?
options: Words, meanings and usage shift across generations, with new words added and others fading
questions.explain: Language evolves as new words appear, meanings shift and some terms become archaic.

questions.q: "Time is a thief that steals our youth." This describing of time AS a thief is a:
questions.explain: Calling time a thief directly, without "like" or "as," is a metaphor.

questions.q: Words such as "however," "meanwhile" and "firstly" that signal the direction of a text are:
questions.explain: Connectives that guide the reader through a text are discourse markers.

questions.q: Which phrase is the clearest example of IMAGERY (language creating a vivid picture)?
options: Crimson leaves drifted onto the frost-glazed path
questions.explain: "Crimson leaves" on a "frost-glazed path" paints a vivid sensory picture, which is imagery.

questions.q: Early in a story, a character nervously eyes a loaded gun on the wall. Hinting at a later event is:
questions.explain: Planting an early hint of something to come is foreshadowing.

questions.q: In a job interview, which language choice is most appropriate?
options: Specialist jargon the interviewer won't know
Standard English with a polite, formal register
questions.explain: Formal contexts like interviews call for Standard English and a polite register.

questions.q: Placing "the richest man in the poorest town" side by side to highlight contrast is:
questions.explain: Positioning contrasting ideas together for effect is juxtaposition.

questions.q: Which feature is typical of spontaneous spoken language but not planned writing?
options: Fillers and false starts like 'um, I mean, the thing is...'
questions.explain: Spontaneous speech often contains fillers, false starts and self-correction.
